text.content:
The Storytellers Guide's "Alternate Storytelling Techniques" chapter covers four tools for running scenes outside normal real-time play: Flashbacks, Flash-Forwards, Dream Sequences, and Blue Books and Downtimes. The first three are pure Storyteller creative-craft advice — how to pick a character and moment, how to keep the scene focused, how to use symbolism — with no dice mechanics, Trait costs, or formal procedure attached, so they aren't reproduced here as rules content. Blue Books and Downtimes, however, describes a genuine structured process for resolving play between sessions, which is documented below since it's something players actively participate in.

Downtimes vs. Blue Books

These are two distinct tools for handling time and action that can't fit into a live session, and the source text is explicit that they are not the same thing:

  • Downtimes are the simpler, more common tool: when several weeks pass between sessions in the chronicle's timeline, the Storyteller asks each player to report how her character spent the intervening time. A good downtime report can reveal a lot about a character's actions and motives, but it's fundamentally a solo effort — it's the player's imagination alone, with no input from other players and no in-the-moment reaction from the Storyteller, so it does not really constitute roleplaying.
  • Blue booking is a genuine collaborative roleplaying process: two or more players (with the Storyteller) build out a scene in writing outside of game time, in a group round-robin format. The Storyteller sets the initial scene; one player writes her character's actions and reactions; the next player edits and adds to it and passes it along; this continues until all participants are satisfied, at which point the finished scene is handed to the Storyteller to fold into the chronicle.

Requirements for a Valid Blue Book Scene

  • All participating players must be mature, self-directed roleplayers — blue booking only works when the Storyteller can trust the group to develop the scene faithfully without direct supervision.
  • It must be a no-challenge scene. The moment a blue book scene would call for a Trait challenge (combat or otherwise contested action), it needs to move to a live, in-person scene with the Storyteller present instead.
  • It's best suited to quiet, low-stakes material — conversations, day-to-day socializing, downtime-style business — not confrontations between rivals or anything plot-critical enough to need adjudication.
  • E-mail (or any similarly fast back-and-forth medium) is a good delivery mechanism, but the Storyteller should encourage players to slow down and put real detail into each pass rather than dashing off quick replies just because the medium allows it; it's the finished draft that matters, not the back-and-forth that produced it.

Storyteller's Role

A properly-run blue book needs almost no moderation once underway: if the players steer the scene somewhere unexpected (e.g., from a coffee shop conversation into a back-alley confrontation), the Storyteller generally lets them, intervening only if the scene threatens to disrupt the wider chronicle or needs to escalate into a challenge (at which point it stops being a blue book and becomes a live scene). Finished blue book scenes are worth keeping on file even after the fact purely as characterization reference, since they tend to reveal how a player thinks through her character's motives.

Both tools are explicitly framed as supplements to, not replacements for, live-action play: Mind's Eye Theatre is meant to be played in person and on one's feet, and players should be encouraged back into real-time scenes as soon as it's practical.
